answer: Assign a globally unique ID to anything that asks for one. As code: write a function (getid()) that returns something unique every single time it is invoked. An ID is whatever gives uniqueness to a row, document, object or event.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'So the problem is easy to say. Assign a globally unique ID to anything that asks for one. Put as code: write a function that returns something unique every single time it is invoked.'

answer: No. It starts as an ID function that is part of your own application/business logic, called locally on every request inside the request handler. A central ID service is an evolution reached later.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Start with an ID function that is part of your own application logic, called locally on every request. A central ID service is an evolution you reach later.' Rule: 'Start with a function, not a service.'

answer: Because time is unique and always moves forward, so the function can just return the current epoch ms (e.g. 1729). It works only on exactly one machine, and only as long as the function is never invoked twice within the same millisecond (otherwise both calls get the same value and you'd have to go to micro/nanoseconds).
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'Time is unique and always moves forward, so the ID function can just return the current epoch millisecond'; 'version 1 is correct on exactly one machine, as long as the code is never called twice within one millisecond.'

answer: Both return the same value, 1729, so the IDs collide and are no longer globally unique. Fix: concatenate the machine ID with the epoch ms: m1-1729 and m2-1729, unique across both (concat(machine_id, get_epoch_ms())).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'Both can run the function within the same millisecond, and both return the same value, 1729... The fix is to concatenate the machine ID with the epoch millisecond: m1-1729 ... m2-1729'

answer: Whenever you see a collision, add to the ID the thing that led to it (two machines collided, so the machine goes into the ID). Then look for a cheaper alternative to adding it (e.g. a counter instead of the thread ID, a flush every N instead of every time).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2 rule: 'Whenever you see a collision, add the thing that led to it. Then look for a cheaper alternative to adding it'

answer: Because of threads: if the program runs threads on several cores, the function can run twice within the same millisecond on the same machine, so two threads both produce m1-1729.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'Threads break it again. If the program runs threads on several cores, the function can run twice within the same millisecond on the same machine, and two threads both produce m1-1729.'

answer: First, append the thread ID (machine ID + thread ID + epoch ms, e.g. m1-t1-1729); second, use an atomically incremented static counter instead of the thread ID.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2–2.3: 'the first fix is to add the thread ID'; 'There is a second way to separate threads. Instead of the thread ID, add a counter'; 'two ways to beat thread collisions: append the thread ID, or use an atomically incremented static counter'

answer: get_id returns concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()); IDs look like m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729 (and m2-t1-1729, m2-t3-1729). Thread IDs are typically integers assigned by the OS; t1, t2 are shorthand.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'func get_id() { return concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()); // m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729 }' and Fig 2·b

answer: Because always appending the thing that led to the conflict leads to gigantic IDs (every new cause makes the ID longer). One counter avoids that and works no matter how many threads there are.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'always appending the thing that led to the conflict leads to gigantic IDs. A counter avoids that.'

answer: One globally allocated variable that every thread can reach: one copy per process, shared by all threads (lecture says think of it as on the heap; strictly static storage duration). Its increment must be atomic/thread-safe — counter++ is not atomic by default, so wrap it in a lock/mutex or use the language's native atomic library (same count++ race as Lecture 2). Then no two threads get the same value.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'The counter is a static counter: one globally allocated variable that every thread can reach... Increment it atomically'; 'The increment must be thread-safe, and counter++ is not atomic by default. Wrap it in a lock or mutex, or use your language’s native atomic library.'

answer: m1-1729-01, m1-1729-02, m1-1729-03, then m1-1730-01 (m1-1730-…) once the millisecond moves on.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'One machine produces m1-1729-01, m1-1729-02, m1-1729-03, then m1-1730-… once the millisecond moves on.' Fig 2·c step 2.

answer: Because the atomically incremented counter already increases (differs) on every call, so the time part adds nothing; with the machine ID in front, machine plus counter is unique on its own. Resulting ID: concat(machine_id, counter++), e.g. m1-01, m1-02, m1-03 (m2-01...).
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'With an atomically increasing counter, the time part is redundant: the counter alone gives 1, 2, 3, … So drop time... machine ID plus counter, m1-01, m1-02, m1-03.'

answer: Size: the counter can hit the integer limit, about 4 billion. With 2^64 it is so massive you might never hit it. (Also, unique only as long as the counter never resets.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'Its one limit is size: the counter can hit the integer limit, which is about 4 billion. With 2^64 it is such a massive number that you might never hit it.'

answer: It resets to 0, so the machine hands out m1-01, m1-02 again — IDs it already issued; no longer unique. Root cause: the counter is stored in volatile memory with no persistence.
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'The static counter lived in volatile memory with no persistence, so it resets to 0, and the machine hands out m1-01, m1-02 again... The root cause is where the counter is stored: volatile memory.'

answer: Back the counter up to a file on disk. At process start, load the counter from disk once; on every call, increment it, immediately save it to disk, then concatenate as before: int counter = load(); get_id(){ counter++; save_counter(counter); return concat(machine_id, counter); }. Board labelled it fault tolerance. (Caveat: a plain write() lands in page cache; fsync() is needed to survive a crash, and that flush is the expensive part.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'when the process starts, load the counter from disk. On every call, increment it, immediately save it to disk... then concatenate as before... labelled fault tolerance' and code block; fsync note.

answer: 1) Disk pressure: a disk IO per ID — at thousands of calls a second the disk takes heavy pressure from many micro disk IOs. 2) Latency: every ID now waits on a disk IO instead of being served from memory.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'Saving the counter on every call means a disk IO per ID... the disk takes a lot of pressure from a great many micro disk IOs. That is problem one. Problem two is latency'

answer: A really good approach because it tackles the disk IO problem head on (written once per startup; nothing written while IDs are handed out). Costs: the increment at startup must be atomic (it can be made atomic), and the ID gets longer (third part) — only the long ID might become a problem, though not a big one (long IDs don't index well, ch. 4).
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'It has two costs. The increment at startup has to be atomic (it can be made atomic), and the ID gets longer. It is a really good approach, because it tackles the disk IO problem head on. Only the long ID might become a problem, though not a big one'

answer: When you read the counter (say 1), add 1000 and store that; then serve IDs from memory, and when you reach the stored value, read and add 1000 again — a thousand IDs per disk write. I.e., write to disk periodically at a certain frequency instead of every time, so disk IOs collapse. Comes back in flush-every-N and in Amazon's ID service.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'The second idea is a bank of IDs. When you read the counter, say it is 1, add 1000 to it and store that. Then serve IDs from memory, and when you reach the stored value, read and add 1000 again'

answer: const N = 1000; int counter = load() + N; func get_id() { counter++; if (counter % N == 0) save_counter(counter); return concat(machine_id, counter); }
evidence: Ch2 §2.6 code: 'const N = 1000; // flush frequency int counter = load() + N; ... counter++; if (counter % N == 0) save_counter(counter); ... return concat(machine_id, counter);'

answer: Because the disk only holds the last flushed value; the counter may have run up to (but not past) the next flush before a crash, so IDs above the on-disk value may already have been issued. Starting at load() would reissue them; load() + N puts you past anything issued before (the first ++ then hands out last flushed + N + 1).
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'At startup the counter starts at load() plus the flush frequency, to stay clear of anything already issued'; example: 'The last value on disk is 6, but 8 was already handed out. Restarting from 6 would generate 7 and 8 again'

answer: By a factor of 1000 (a massive performance gain). Implement it simply with a mod operation: count, take counter mod N, write — add a periodicity factor; don't reach for a thread with a timer.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'That cuts disk IO by a factor of 1000, a massive performance gain'; 'keep it as simple as a mod operation: count, take the counter mod N, write. Don’t reach for a thread with a timer.'

answer: On disk: 3 (flushed at 03), then 6 (flushed at 06); last value on disk is 6 while 8 was handed out. Safe restart: last flushed + flush frequency + 1 = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10, so it hands out m1-10, m1-11, m1-12 (flushing again at 12). Restarting from 6 would reissue 7 and 8.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6 and Clip 2·1: 'the disk holds 3, then 6... Restarting from the safest value, the last flushed value plus the flush interval plus one, 6 + 3 + 1 = 10, starts at m1-10'

answer: Some integers are never handed out: here m1-09 (had the crash come before 8 went out, both 8 and 9 would be lost). Acceptable because correctness of the system matters more than using every integer: an unused number is fine, a duplicate ID is not.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'Some integers are never handed out: here, m1-09... That is fine. The correctness of the system matters more than using every single integer.' Clip: 'An unused number is fine. A duplicate ID is not.'

answer: 1) Don't do IO every time: add a periodicity factor, as simple as a mod operation (not a timer thread). 2) Whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value — always think of correctness first.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'First, don’t do IO every time. Add a periodicity factor... Second, whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value. Always think of correctness first.'

answer: For conflict resolution (one place they're needed, not the only one). Example: airline check-in from Lecture 3 — transactions T1 and T2 numbered 1 and 2 tell which came first. If a row has a = 10, T1 sets 20, T2 sets 30, with newer-write-wins the larger ID (2) marks the newer write, so accept T2's value, a = 30.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'Think back to the airline check-in in Lecture 3... two transactions write the same row. It holds a = 10; T1 sets it to 20 and T2 sets it to 30... the larger number, 2, marks the newer write, so you accept T2’s value.'

answer: No. 1 2 3 4 5 6 is what the lecture calls strictly monotonically increasing; 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 is (just) monotonically increasing — each new ID is greater than all before it, gaps allowed. Gap-free is the stronger 'sequential' property.
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'Monotonically increasing doesn’t mean purely sequential. The lecture calls 1 2 3 4 5 6 strictly monotonically increasing, and 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 (just) monotonically increasing'

answer: Time moves forward and now sits in the most significant digits, so IDs get a natural order (1729 0001, 1729 0002, 1730 0001); the right half (machine ID or counter) only breaks ties. Pretty decent but not strict. Board: 'all ID generation algorithms have time on LHS', under the word sortability.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'concatenate time first, then the machine ID... it sits in the most significant digits, so the IDs get a natural order'; 'The class board put it as “all ID generation algorithms have time on LHS”, under the word sortability.'

answer: Within one millisecond the order can flip: if the first request goes to machine 2 and the next to machine 1, you get 17290002 then 17290001. Only once the millisecond passes are IDs almost monotonically increasing.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'Within one millisecond the order can still flip. If the first request goes to machine 2 and the next one to machine 1, you get 17290002 first and then 17290001.'

answer: It costs almost nothing: the design stays stateless, so a request can go to any machine, no central state to maintain, throughput stays excellent (you accept a little incorrectness). Plus rough sortability.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'The design is still stateless, so a request can go to any machine; there is no central state to maintain, and throughput stays excellent. In exchange you accept a little incorrectness.'

answer: SRE and DevOps teams run a process that keeps syncing machines' clocks with NTP servers — a periodic job, run more often than you think (in practice a daemon like chronyd, ntpd, systemd-timesyncd that can slew or step the clock).
evidence: Ch3 §3.4: 'SRE and DevOps teams run a process that keeps syncing the machines’ clocks with NTP servers'; 'a periodic job has to keep clocks in sync, and it runs more often than you think.'

answer: A machine's clock is a hardware clock: a quartz crystal vibrates at a frequency and the machine counts vibrations. Physical effects nudge it — the lecture's reasoning: heat (e.g. a high-intensity game) makes the crystal vibrate faster so the clock runs fast; extreme cold slows it. (Page's correction: frequency varies with temperature but not in one direction — a common crystal loses accuracy at both high and low temperatures, ~±20 ppm, parabola ~0.04 ppm/°C² around 25 °C.)
evidence: Ch3 §3.4: 'Because a machine’s clock is a hardware clock. A quartz crystal vibrates...'; 'More precisely: Quartz frequency does vary with temperature... but not in one direction'

answer: IDs (time then machine): 232, 244, 237, 239. They are not monotonically increasing: machine 4's clock is ahead, so 244 is followed by the smaller 237 — arrival order and ID order no longer match; where order is needed, clock skew affects correctness.
evidence: Ch3 §3.5: 'The IDs come out 232, 244, 237, 239. They are not monotonically increasing.' Check yourself: 'The pair 244 then 237 breaks it'

answer: Google's Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat chased a bug that turned out to be a bit flipped by a natural phenomenon (lecture said an explosion or a solar storm). Recommended article remembered as 'the friendship that made Google special' (actually The New Yorker's 'The Friendship That Made Google Huge', 2018). Point: you cannot run away from nature.
evidence: Ch3 §3.4 'You can’t run away from nature' box

answer: Ensuring strict monotonicity across a distributed system where the ID logic runs on many machines is almost impossible — not a theoretical proof, but in practice too many things can break it. Wherever monotonicity is needed, clock skew must be taken care of because it affects correctness.
evidence: Ch3 §3.5: 'Ensuring strict monotonicity across a distributed system, where the ID logic runs on many machines, is almost impossible. That is not a theoretical proof... but in practice too many things can break it.'

answer: One machine hands out every ID: whoever wants an ID makes a network call to the ID server, which runs the same get_id() with one clock, generates an ID and sends it back (clients 1 and 2 calling it; bubble 'my clock never goes back'). Throughput set aside. Motivation: a central ID service should solve the clock-skew problem.
evidence: Ch3 §3.6 and Fig 3·d: 'a central ID generation service: one machine, and whoever wants an ID makes a network call to it'

answer: One machine has one clock, so no skew between generators. When NTP finds the clock ahead (reads 24, should be 23), the clock doesn't jump back; it slows its counting until real time catches up, then carries on from 24 — 'the clock never goes back in time'. (Caveat: true for small offsets which are slewed (<128 ms in ntpd); larger offsets are stepped and the wall clock can jump back, so generators must detect a backward step and wait/refuse, as Snowflake does, or use a monotonic clock.)
evidence: Ch3 §3.6: 'When NTP sync finds the clock is ahead, reading 24 when it should read 23, the clock doesn’t jump back. It slows its counting until real time catches up' + More precisely notes

answer: It is a single point of failure (server or its disk could fail). First fix: add one more ID server behind a load balancer (as in Lecture 5) for fault tolerance.
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'The one ID server is a single point of failure: the server could fail, or its disk could. So for fault tolerance you add one more machine behind a load balancer'

answer: Whichever server gets a request must first talk to the other to see the last ID it generated, add some buffer, then generate — the two must gossip constantly so each new ID is larger than any ever generated. Cost: turns a simple function super complex, loses throughput; continuous gossip at high throughput becomes very messy ('we made the entire process super complicated').
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'whichever server gets a request has to talk to the other ID server first... add some buffer... The two servers have to gossip constantly... it loses throughput'

answer: 'There is no way to distribute and guarantee strict monotonicity.' (You can't have a distributed ID service that also guarantees strict monotonicity at high throughput.)
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'The lesson the class board boxed: “There is no way to distribute and guarantee strict monotonicity.”'

answer: Because MySQL is a single machine, not distributed, and the ID logic is part of its database engine — one engine owns the counter, so 1,2,3,4,5,6 (though not gap-free: InnoDB doesn't reuse values after rollback). In multi-master mode with auto-increment you get many conflicts: each master is its own brain (masters don't talk, each counts 1,2,3,4). MySQL's own fix (Group Replication multi-primary) sets increment 7 and offset = server ID: uniqueness, not order.
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'It does, because MySQL is a single machine... the ID logic is part of its database engine'; 'Put it in multi-master mode... look at the number of conflicts you get: each master is its own brain.' Ch1 §1.2.

answer: Ask whether you really need each constraint; challenge them with critical questions: Is it OK if IDs aren't integers? Random like UUIDs/GUIDs? Not monotonic? Often after a couple of critical questions it turns out monotonicity isn't needed, because not everyone thinks it through. Everything is a trade-off.
evidence: Ch3 §3.8: 'ask whether you really need each constraint. Challenge them with critical questions. Is it OK if IDs are not integers? If they are random...? If they are not monotonic?'

answer: Because once databases are sharded or run multi-master (e.g. two MySQL masters both accepting writes), the servers don't talk to each other and each auto-increments 1,2,3,4 on its own, so IDs collide. You can no longer rely on DB IDs and need your own ID logic (e.g. including machine ID). Also: most hit this at scale, sooner than they think.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'Shard the database, or run it multi-master... each auto-increments 1, 2, 3, 4 on its own, and the IDs collide. Once your databases run multi-master, you can no longer rely on the IDs they hand out.'

answer: No. It would be unique, but that database is still a single machine: it has itself become the shared service — one and the same thing.
evidence: Ch3 §3.6: 'What about a shared database with locks, instead of a shared ID service? It would be unique. But that database is still a single machine: it has itself become the shared service. One and the same thing.'

answer: The counter was there for monotonicity, which a random ID doesn't give. UUIDs can be used if it's OK to relax the monotonicity constraint (not everyone needs it) — but you lose ordering: you get some, you lose some.
evidence: Ch3 §3.8: 'Why a counter in chapter 2 and not a random suffix? The counter was there for monotonicity... in reality you can often relax that constraint, and then a random ID like a UUID works.'

answer: Also correct (unique); it loses monotonicity, and that is fine.
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'Another idea: a distributed set of ID servers, each appending its own server ID to the IDs it generates. That is also correct. It loses monotonicity, and that is fine.'

answer: That is load() by another name — loading from disk or DB is the same, you start from that point. It also quietly assumes every generated ID is written to the database so the max row is the last ID; the logic deliberately doesn't assume that because writing back to the DB is expensive and many IDs are never written anywhere (e.g. request IDs passed along).
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'read the largest ID already stored in the database... In fact that is load() by another name... it quietly assumes an entry is written to the database for every ID generated'

answer: Amazon assigns a globally unique ID to every order; high throughput, and the same ID service hands out IDs to many internal services (orders, payments...), so IDs must be unique. Core idea: batching — instead of calling the remote ID service for every ID, a server gets a batch (range) of IDs in one call (like §2.6 flush-every-N).
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'Amazon assigns a globally unique ID to every order placed... the same ID service also hands out IDs to many other internal services'; 'the server gets a batch of IDs in one call.'

answer: Plain API servers exposing ID-generation endpoints, behind a load balancer, with a classic relational database behind them (table id_ranges with one counter row per service, e.g. orders, payments). No fancy non-relational store.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'plain API servers exposing ID-generation endpoints, put behind a load balancer, with a database behind them. That database is a classic relational one.' Fig 5·a.

answer: No. Neither cares about monotonicity; they need uniqueness only.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'Neither cares about monotonicity. They need uniqueness, as simple as that.'

answer: Server 1 gets [0, 500) and the orders counter moves 0 → 500; server 2 gets [500, 1000) and the counter goes to 1000. Only start and end are returned, not 500 individual IDs.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2 Fig 5·a steps 1–2: 'One update moves the orders counter from 0 to 500 and returns the range [0, 500)'; 'the counter goes to 1000 and server 2 holds [500, 1000).'

answer: Atomically: in a transaction, SELECT the current counter FOR UPDATE (locked), then UPDATE it to counter + batch size, COMMIT, and reply with old and new value as the range — same as Lecture 3's airline check-in transaction.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'Select the current value FOR UPDATE inside a transaction, then update it to the new value... it is Lecture 3’s airline check-in transaction' + SQL block

answer: Decoupling: ID generation is separate from the orders DB, so the orders database can be sharded and scaled horizontally with every shard accepting writes; servers pull IDs from their in-memory range and write to their own orders DB without calling the ID service per ID.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'the central ID service decouples the system... the orders database can be sharded and scaled horizontally, with every shard accepting writes'

answer: Real batches: 10,000, 50,000 or 100,000 IDs, depending on the service's throughput. Trade-off: too small and servers make network calls too often; too large and a crash throws away a big range. Each service tunes its max batch size to its throughput.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'real batches are 10,000, 50,000 or 100,000 IDs... too small, and servers make network calls too often; too large, and a crash throws away a big range.'

answer: It refills before running out: e.g. with 490 of 500 used it asks for another 500 and gets whatever range is next (e.g. [3000, 3500), since other servers took ranges in between), then carries on from that range.
evidence: Ch5 §5.2: 'with 490 of its 500 used, it asks for another 500 and might get 3000–3500, because other servers took the ranges in between.'

answer: No order across servers (server 1 may issue 3,042 while server 2 issues 612); it only promises unique IDs. It scales easily because the DB is the single source of truth on a single server, never gossips, and each request is one tiny update (not even a full read), once per batch.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'there is no order across servers... It is really simple to build. The database is the single source of truth on a single server, so it never has to gossip... each request is one tiny update'

answer: No. Tracking every used ID is a massive overhead, and a big-integer (2^64) ID space will never run out even at Amazon's scale; losing a few ranges (e.g. 9,900 of a 10,000 batch) doesn't matter. Think about practicality.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3: 'In fact it isn’t worth it. Keeping track of every single used ID is a massive overhead, and a big-integer (2^64) ID space will never run out'

answer: The difference between a million and a billion is 999 million — itself almost a billion. A 4-byte integer gives about 4 billion IDs (≈4.29 billion unsigned; signed 32-bit about 2.1 billion) — imagine 4 billion Amazon orders; if that runs out, move to 64 bits.
evidence: Ch5 §5.3 Number sense: 'the difference between them, 999 million, is itself almost a billion. A four-byte integer gives about 4 billion IDs'

answer: 128 bits (16 bytes). Avoided at scale because it's extremely inefficient for indexes: every index entry stores the ID, so a 16-byte ID bloats indexes (~4× vs 4-byte INT, ~2× vs BIGINT; e.g. 1 GB → 4 GB rough estimate), and indexes need to fit in RAM; random v4 UUIDs also land at random places (poor index locality).
evidence: Ch4 §4.1–4.2: 'a UUID is: a 128-bit value'; 'Switch from one to the other and you bloat the index by a factor of four'; random v4 'have poor database-index locality'

answer: Because the query execution plan is built on the indexes; if indexes fit in RAM, the whole plan (e.g. joins on indexed columns) runs in memory and only result rows are read from disk last. If indexes spill to disk, every lookup becomes a disk read and no other optimization makes it fast. (Precisely: the hot part must fit in the buffer pool.)
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'the first thing it does is build a query execution plan, and it does that work on the indexes... If they fit in RAM... Only once it knows the result does it go to the disk'; 'If it can’t, no amount of other optimization will make it fast.'

answer: Check index size first (usually random indexes were created and spilled to disk). DB server RAM should be equal to or more than total index size — bare minimum memory = sum of all index sizes; beyond is good. (In practice size the buffer pool for hot indexes/data, RAM larger since cache gets ≤ ~80%.)
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'when a database is slow, check index size first'; 'the RAM of your database server should be equal to or more than your total index size'; 'the bare minimum memory is the sum of the sizes of all the indexes'

answer: They look random and can't be predicted, so it's hard to guess other IDs or scrape the whole site — good for security in that sense (vs plain 1,2,3 IDs scraped by a loop). Caveat: not a security control; access checks still needed. Also unique with no coordination.
evidence: Ch4 §4.4: 'They look random, and you can’t predict the next one, so it is hard for anyone to guess other IDs or scrape your whole website.'

answer: No. UUIDs aren't forbidden; if your app is small and will never hit that scale, a UUID is just fine. Don't reach for the best solution by default; see what works for you.
evidence: Ch4 §4.4: 'So UUIDs are not forbidden... If your application is small and will never hit that scale, a UUID is just fine.'

answer: 12 bytes (96 bits): first 4 bytes epoch time (seconds) — time first; then 5 random bytes; then a 3-byte counter. (Older layout had machine ID and process ID where random bytes are.)
evidence: Ch4 §4.5: 'ObjectIds, are 12 bytes: the first 4 bytes are epoch time... then 5 random bytes; then a 3-byte counter.' Fig 4·c.

answer: 4 or 8 bytes is fine (MySQL 4-byte auto-increment gives a very tiny index); beyond 8 bytes you should worry about performance at scale.
evidence: Ch4 §4.5: 'Four bytes or eight is still fine; beyond eight bytes you should worry about performance at scale.'

answer: Flickr's database was sharded and multi-master, so writes could go anywhere and auto-increment on every shard would produce conflicting IDs; to guarantee uniqueness it needed its own ID generation. Not UUIDs because they index badly.
evidence: Ch5 §5.5: 'The database was sharded and ran in multi-master mode... auto-increment on every shard would hand out conflicting IDs... why not UUIDs: they index badly'

answer: Because it's where everything is stored and queried and it handles the entire load; API servers are easy to scale since they're mostly stateless, but the database is not. (Lecture 2: most critical and most brittle.) So understand your database really well.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'The database is the most essential, and the most brutal, component of an infrastructure. API servers are easy to scale because they are mostly stateless... The database is where everything is stored and everything is queried; it handles the entire load.'

answer: Table tickets: id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, primary key; stub CHAR(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT '', with a UNIQUE KEY. Holds one row (e.g. id 74, stub 'a').
evidence: Ch5 §5.5 and Fig 5·c: 'create table tickets ( id bigint unsigned not null auto_increment, stub char(1) not null default '', primary key (id), unique key (stub) );'

answer: If MySQL already gives auto-increment IDs, let MySQL itself be the ID service: a separate ticket database with one table/one row; whoever needs an ID queries it. Naive way is delete row + insert new (auto-increment fills next value), but delete-then-insert in a transaction is extremely costly on the database; instead use one upsert statement.
evidence: Ch5 §5.5–5.6: 'why can’t MySQL itself be the ID service?'; 'Delete-then-insert can run in one transaction, but that is extremely costly on the database. Or it can become an upsert'

answer: 1) INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE: tries the insert; if it fails on a unique key, runs the given update (classic upsert). 2) REPLACE INTO: also upserts but internally deletes the old row and inserts a new one (unlisted columns reset to defaults, fires DELETE and INSERT triggers), so it's slower — a first-hand benchmark found it about 32× slower (one measurement).
